Technical Communication Essentials
My name is Chinenye Precious Anyasor, and I have a bachelor's in human physiology. By now, I thought I would be working in a lab somewhere, but alas, life had its plans.
These are the tools I used to write, design, and publish my portfolio.

This would be a long read; please bear with me. Over the years, I have seen different variations of this quote: “You aren't lost; you're just in an uncomfortable stage of your life where your old self is gone, but your new self isn't fully born yet. You're in the midst of transformation.” At some point, I may have even posted it on my WhatsApp status. I always thought I understood its meaning until I lived and experienced it. And perhaps, it taught me my biggest lessons this year. I finished my university education in December 2022. While waiting for my clearance, I worked at my sister’s boutique. I was earning money, but I was anxious about my future. I did not know what to do with my life or how to turn the big dreams I had “dreamt up” in school into reality. It did not help that I studied a course that could not translate into a job or anything with any semblance of one. It’s one of those courses where you only realise you made a huge mistake studying it during your matriculation. By 2023, it was clear I had a very real problem. I had finished clearance and still didn’t know what to do with my life. I had started applying for entry-level corporate positions, but never heard back from any of them. This was with my then caricature of a CV. I was under a lot of pressure. It felt like time for me to be somebody was quickly running out, and I was playing catch-up. That was until I saw PiggyVest’s opening for a People Operations Associate. I knew I could not apply; I did not have the requisite experience. But for the first time, I was intrigued by a career path. I read through the job ad thoroughly and went further to read about HR in general, how to get into the field, where to take courses, and what books to read. Before I knew it, I had completed three courses, volunteered for some organisations, and was looking for my first opportunity. I had also used some LinkedIn profiles to map out what my career could look like if I stayed the course. The skills I needed to have a grasp of. The proper certifications to take. You know, the whole nine yards. The point is, I was so sure that HR was my life’s mission, my life’s work. By the end of 2023, I got my first HR opportunity as an HR assistant. Oh, I gave it my all and then some. After all, my life’s work deserved nothing short of the best. It got to a point where my manager, the head of HR, who was going on maternity leave, decided not to hire an experienced interim as planned because she was convinced I could handle it. And so, for the next three months, I was the interim HR manager of an organisation with a workforce of over 400. By the end of that period, I was promoted to an HR Generalist, with rumours of a possible talent manager promotion. This was all within two years. Life should be good, right? It was not. Beneath all that work, I would occasionally catch myself feeling dissatisfied and asking if that was it. But I was always either too busy or too tired to give it proper thought. By June 2025, I resigned from the job. I was thoroughly burned out. My capacity to perform struggled to keep up with the growth I was experiencing. More importantly, life had become so busy that I no longer had time for the things that brought me joy. The very things that allowed me to show up at work the way I did. So I left, deciding to rest properly before re-entering the job market. During that quiet, dissatisfaction crept up again. Surely, what I had experienced at my last job could not be it. Shortly after, I started job hunting. By the start of this year (2026), I had gotten a senior People Operations role that 2023 me would have been over the moon for. A good salary, real exposure to leadership, an opportunity to learn stakeholder management and work in a tech environment that offered real exposure to AI. Yet, I wasn’t excited, and I could not pinpoint why. Anyways, I took the job. A girl has got to eat, you know. But as soon as I began, I knew I had made a terrible mistake. I was miserable. Something was off, but what exactly? I had no idea. I found myself calling my senior colleagues to ask them what was next. Was that it? They all gave variations of plans for climbing the HR career ladder. But I think what I really wanted was permission to leave that seemingly perfect job and to understand my sudden lack of interest in HR, which was fast becoming a lack of interest in everything too. I eventually left because I felt I was not giving my best. And I wasn’t, and still am not, the girl who doesn’t give her best. That has never been me. I still thank God for the privilege of having been able to leave. Retrospectively, I think that was the point I let go of that version of myself and her dreams. Then came the real anxiety. I had perpetual low energy; nothing brought me joy, and all I wanted to do was sleep. I kept reaching for anything and anyone that would make sense. The recurring question became: why was this happening to me? I was in that state of mind for a major part of this year. I was also chronically online, watching what felt like thousands of videos on what to do when you don’t know what to do with your life. It felt like 2023 all over again. Only this time, it felt worse because I actually had an amazing job and had just let it go. Anyways, watching those videos left me more confused than I already was. I desperately needed to hear my own thoughts. So, as my last act of hope, I left all social media platforms. LinkedIn included. I downloaded Substack, just to read and write. Those were the only things that made sense. After some time, I realised that even though I may not have known exactly what I wanted to do, I knew it had to do with writing. It was the one constant in my life, from keeping journals in secondary school and through university to growing my LinkedIn account to over 13,000 followers, just by writing about my experiences as I learnt HR. I tried ghostwriting, built a portfolio and set up a whole system, but it never went beyond that. Then I tried proposal and grant writing. It also did not go anywhere, due to my lack of interest, I presume. You must know that all my life, my effort has always been in the direction of my interest. Always. It was and still is my litmus test for the things I want out of life. Well, I soldiered on until the day I had a conversation with ChatGPT about technical writing. I can't remember where I heard about it first, but I remember having an insatiable appetite for reading anything and everything related to the field. Before I knew it, I was done with The Insider’s Guide to Technical Writing by Krista Van Laan. An incredible book, as an aside. It led me to join the Write the Docs Slack community for tech writers. Soon, I had completed a three-course specialisation on Coursera. I had also written a four-part user guide on getting started on a stock trading app called Meritrade, including FAQs and a style guide, as my unofficial portfolio samples. All written with Markdown in VS Code. What's funny is that I can’t remember the exact day or time when my world started to feel right again. When I started feeling like me. When everything seemed to be in its place and I stopped feeling confused about life. I genuinely cannot remember. It's almost like I woke up one day and found all this evidence of what I had been pouring my energy into for the past couple of months. Clearly, I am not the same girl from January. That girl is long gone, and that's fine because I really like her replacement. Not just because she swapped dreams, but because of the changes she has made in other aspects of her life too. So, my takeaways? Firstly, I now know enough to understand that just because someone explains their experience to me in a language we both speak and understand, whether verbally or in a written format like a quote, does not mean I truly understand it. There is a certain level of empathy or perspective I can never have until the experience is a shared one. Secondly, there was no way I could have known that I was between versions of myself. We only recognise it retrospectively, after we have settled into a new version of ourselves. It's beyond our control. I suspect I have a few more versions of myself to get through. So, in the future, I will pay attention, allow myself to go through it, feel my feelings like my friend would always advise, and not always try to make sense of things. Also, while writing that last sentence, I realised I had experienced this earlier in life, when my first relationship ended, along with everything I thought I wanted from one. I think the lesson life has been desperately trying to teach me is that I am allowed to change my mind. About people, beliefs, ideas and things. I am allowed to outgrow relationships, convictions, ambitions and even things I once worked incredibly hard to become. Changing my mind does not mean I was wrong to have wanted those things in the first place. And it certainly isn't evidence that something is wrong with me. I think I've finally accepted that. And I think you should too.

documents.t: For decades, organizations in different sectors have carefully set up systems that cover the supply, training, and eventual retention of entry-level employees. In some sectors, this system is formal and highly standardized, like graduate trainee programmes, which involve job rotations, mentorship, simulations and defined learning pathways. This is particularly popular in the banking sector. In other sectors, the system is less formal. In some cases, the mandatory one-year NYSC supplies entry-level workers, while training happens informally through intentional mentorship and training provided by assigned managers. These systems, whether formal or less formal, when done right, have been successful in producing solid entry-level employees who go on to become the experienced professionals needed to replace mid-level workers as they move up the career ladder or move on to other things. This is how organizations have ensured a cycle of continuity in the workforce. For example, my first professional job after school was in a multinational with over 400 employees. I worked as an HR intern in the Human Resources department. It turned out that a lot of the work I had to do involved using spreadsheets (Microsoft Excel), and I had no prior experience with the software. I had to learn. My manager recommended online resources, and with the help of the company’s Data Analyst, I was able to get up to speed. I also remember being assigned work that involved a lot of research. I would spend hours moving from one website to another, looking for articles relevant to my research. I remember being advised to maintain an empty Word document where I could save relevant links and also use it for brainstorming. Sometimes, the work required me to compare employee benefits and prepare detailed reports for management. My drafts would usually go through several rounds of review before the final document was approved for presentation. On some days, I would spend all night preparing PowerPoint slides, designing graphics to celebrate employee milestones, or editing videos after a team bonding activity. All of these were in addition to the responsibilities in my actual job description. I will be honest: I hated the entry-level phase of my career. I hated the grunt work that came with it. It was not glamorous, but it taught me how to work. It taught me to use tools I was not familiar with before and to sit with the discomfort of not getting something right the first time until I did. It taught me how to synthesize information, think critically, and exercise good judgment. It taught me many of the things that make me a good mid-level professional today. This is the ROI organizations get for investing in entry-level workers: a continuous supply of experienced professionals to fill gaps as mid-level workers move up and senior professionals retire. Well, fast forward to today. AI has entered the conversation, with the capacity to give us far more for less in minutes. With the right prompts, research, PowerPoint slides, video editing, automation of repetitive tasks, data analysis, writing, document editing, graphic design, and much more can now be done in minutes. And organizations, in a bid to optimize for efficiency and minimize costs, introduced AI into the very system they created to ensure they always have capable talent. General tasks that were once associated with entry-level roles are now being handled by AI. In specific fields, AI has also changed the way work is done. For example, AI has been introduced into various aspects of recruitment and software development, where it has given rise to what is commonly called vibe coding. Today, AI can even join a meeting as a participant, give updates, receive feedback, and use that feedback to iterate on assigned work, much like an actual employee. The result is that, in some fields and organizations, AI is reducing the need for certain junior roles or the number of people required to perform tasks previously assigned to them. And where entry-level positions still exist, the nature of the work has changed. There is already some research pointing to this shift. A working paper by researchers at Stanford University's Digital Economy Lab, using payroll data covering millions of US workers, found that employment among young workers aged 22 to 25 in occupations highly exposed to AI was 19% below the level it would have reached if it had grown at the same rate as employment in less AI-exposed occupations. Interestingly, the researchers attributed much of this difference to reduced hiring of young workers rather than increased layoffs. A separate analysis by the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, using US Census Bureau data, found a similar pattern: employment among younger workers in highly AI-exposed occupations had declined, with fewer young people moving into these jobs. While these findings do not establish that AI is solely responsible for the decline, they point to a growing concern: the impact of AI may be felt not only through the jobs it replaces, but also through the entry-level opportunities organizations no longer create. So the question is, in light of the not-so-recent changes brought about by AI, how do we ensure continuity in the workforce when the system previously designed to train entry-level employees and develop solid professionals has been changed unintentionally? In my opinion, I do not think the introduction of AI is the problem. The issue is that organizations have failed to go back to the drawing board to redesign the systems used to train entry-level employees and rethink how work is structured in light of AI usage. We need to find a way to ensure the coexistence of innovations such as AI and entry-level roles. It should never be one or the other, as is happening today. Also, the onus is not just on organizations. This responsibility extends to schools as well. The making of a solid professional does not start with or depend solely on the training provided to entry-level employees by organizations. It starts way before that, in school. Students who will be expected to use AI at work in the future should be encouraged to start using it in school. This preparation should begin long before they become entry-level employees. Yes, I know this is not straightforward. There are risks to consider, and that is a whole different conversation. The point is that school curricula should change as frequently as needed to accommodate the realities of the job market. I have also found that curriculum review practices vary across education systems. According to an OECD report, some countries undertake major curriculum reforms as needed, while others follow fixed cycles, commonly between five and ten years. In Nigeria, for instance, the NUC recommends that engineering and technology programmes be reviewed at least once every five years. However, given the pace of technological change and its impact on the job market, I think institutions need to pay closer attention to how frequently their curricula are reviewed, updated, and implemented. Anyway, all of this is to help us recognize that we all have a collective responsibility. The consequences of continuing on this path could be a future with retired senior professionals, few or no mid-level professionals to replace them, and unemployed entry-level workers. AI is not the enemy, and frankly, I think it is here to stay. So instead of spending time coming up with think pieces (no offence to those who write them) focused on telling entry-level workers how to adapt to today's market, we should all begin to think about the changes that need to happen at a systemic level to ensure that the workforce remains self-replenishing.

documents.t: Introduction​ Nigeria has come a long way with payments. From manual bank payments, where we queued for hours, to early mobile/internet banking, to the rise of online payments that fuelled the explosion of online shopping. You can buy anything online these days, from foodstuff to gadgets, without leaving your home, yet many people don't know how online payments work and often wonder how they work. Well, you are about to find out. To fully understand how online payments work, you need to understand payment service providers, payment gateways, and webhooks.

Nigeria has come a long way with payments. From manual bank payments, where we queued for hours, to early mobile/internet banking, to the rise of online payments that fuelled the explosion of online shopping. You can buy anything online these days, from foodstuff to gadgets, without leaving your home, yet many people don't know how online payments work and often wonder how they work. Well, you are about to find out. To fully understand how online payments work, you need to understand payment service providers, payment gateways, and webhooks.

They are companies that own and provide the technology (payment gateway and payment processor) businesses use to collect payments from customers online. They make it possible for you to shop and pay online. Some of them include: Paystack, Flutterwave, PayU, Seerbit and others.

A payment gateway is the technology that lets a business accept online payments. It securely collects and encrypts a customer’s payment details at checkout, whether by card, bank transfer, or another method, and passes them to the payment processor, which completes the transaction with the customer’s bank. The exact steps through which this happens are a bit complicated and different for each online payment option, but let's look at how a card payment works. Sarah’s clothing vendor is running a website sale. To shop, she opens the website, selects a few items, chooses card payment, enters her card details, and completes the payment. To walk through the process by which the payment gateway ensures Sarah’s payment gets to her vendor, you need to understand the following:​ Encryption: this process secures Sarah’s card details so only the necessary parties can access them. Issuing bank: this is Sarah’s bank; she has an account with them. They issued the debit and credit card whose details she entered during checkout. Payment Processor: the part of the payment service provider that receives encrypted card details from the payment gateway, sends them to the issuing bank for authorization, and returns an approval or decline. Authorization: the process by which Sarah’s bank checks whether she has enough funds in her account for the items she wants to buy and whether her account has any restrictions. Acquiring bank: this is the bank that receives and holds payment made through a debit or credit card on behalf of the payment service provider till they send it to Sarah’s vendor’s account. Settlement: this is when Sarah’s bank moves the required amount from her account to the payment service provider’s bank, called the acquiring bank. Now that we are familiar with these concepts, let’s walk through the simplified version of how a payment gateway ensures that Sarah’s vendor receives her payment.​ The gateway receives Sarah’s card details and encrypts them. The gateway sends the encrypted data to the provider’s payment processor. The payment processor sends an authorization request to the issuing bank (Sarah’s bank). The issuing bank checks Sarah’s account to see whether it has enough funds to cover the items she wants to buy. It also checks that her account isn't frozen or restricted due to fraud. The issuing bank approves or declines the payment based on the results of these checks. The payment processor passes the result back to the gateway, which shows Sarah a message on her screen: “Payment successful” or “Payment failed.” At the same time, the payment service provider sends a webhook to the vendor’s server, so the vendor knows the payment went through and can process Sarah’s order. Later, usually within a day or two, the issuing bank (Sarah’s bank) sends the required amount to the payment service provider’s acquiring bank. This transfer is called settlement. The payment service provider sends the money to Sarah’s vendor’s bank account.

In step 7, we mentioned a webhook. Let’s look at it from the vendor’s perspective. How does Sarah’s vendor find out that her payment was successful? That’s where a webhook comes in. A webhook is an automated message from a payment service provider to the vendor’s server. It is sent when something happens on the provider’s platform that affects the vendor, such as a payment succeeding or failing, a settlement being made, or a refund being issued, among others.
Now you understand the basics of how online payments work, from the role of payment service providers and payment gateways to how webhooks keep businesses informed about transactions.

Meritrade is an online stock trading app owned and controlled by Meristem, used to buy and sell stocks on the Nigerian stock exchange, provide up-to-date market insights, and let users set up a watchlist for stocks of interest so they never miss an opportunity to buy or sell. This guide walks you through the steps required to buy stocks on Meritrade.

Log in to your Meritrade account​ An image showing the Log in page Enter your email address and password to log in to your Meritrade account. Click on New Trade​ An image showing the location of New Trade on homepage Select Buy​ An image showing the location of Buy Click on Select stock​ An image showing the search bar to be used to locate stock tickers Use the search bar to locate the specific stock you want to buy. Enter the quantity of stock you want to buy​ An image showing where you indicate the quantity of stocks you want to buy As you enter the quantity of stock you want to buy, the price is reflected. Click on Select Portfolio​ An image showing where you select your portfolio When you created your Meritrade account, you were automatically assigned a portfolio. Select it. Select Order Type​ An image showing the different order types There are two types of orders: Market Order: this is an instruction to buy the stock immediately at the best available price. Select this order if you want to buy the stock immediately, regardless of price. Limit Order: this is an instruction to buy only if the price gets to a certain level specified by you. Select this order when you want to buy a stock when it s at a specific price. Important Be mindful of when you plan to buy stock(s); try to buy when the market is still open. If you buy stock(s) after the market closes or before it opens, kindly note that you will only be able to place a limit order. Select Order Term​ An image showing where to select Order Term Order term specifies how long your order is valid for. For example, if you place a limit order with a 1-day term and the price you wanted isn't reached within that day, the order becomes invalid at the end of the day. Click on Preview order​ An image showing where to click to preview your order An image showing the preview Preview your order to ensure everything is correct. You also see the additional cost that comes with buying stocks, such as broker commission and regulatory fees. Click on BUY​ An image showing the BUY button Once you click on BUY, you will receive a copy of your trade order and a contract note in your email linked to Meritrade. Click on Back to home​ An image showing that your order was successful Once the order has been successfully placed, you will see a message saying, Trade Order Placed Successfully.

I took several technical communication courses and wanted to practice what I learned. I chose an app and created four user guides for Meritrade, a stock-trading platform. They cover: Creating an account Funding an account Buying stocks Selling stocks I also included an FAQ section as part of my unofficial portfolio project.
The guide is written for end users who, regardless of their investing experience, have never used Meritrade and aren't familiar with its user interface (UI).

Identified my users. Researched the product and the workflows I wanted to document by using the product myself. Wrote down my first draft in Markdown in VS Code. Annotated screenshots in Greenshot for the guides. Edited the guides against my style guide built from patterns I caught in my drafts. Version-controlled the guides with Git and published them on GitHub.

Early on, each guide had its own top-level image folder. As the suite grew to four guides, I restructured to a single images/ folder with a subfolder per guide. It’s a small choice, but it helps anyone browsing the repo see one clear system instead of four similar ones. This consistency reflects my goals for the writing and the file structure. I picked ‘stocks’ over ‘shares’ early and used it everywhere, across all four guides. Switching between the two in the middle of a document or suite might confuse readers. They could think the terms mean different things. Using one consistent term removes that doubt. I felt torn between adding an FAQ inside each guide and creating a standalone FAQ section. I chose the latter. I wanted all answers in one place. This way, the task guides stayed short and focused. Plus, it made updating one page easier.

While documenting the workflow for creating a Meritrade account, the phone verification step failed. I was supposed to receive an OTP to verify my phone number, but I didn't. Despite clicking Resend OTP several times, I still didn’t receive the OTP. I contacted the support team, but they didn’t respond that day. So I started the account creation process again, but found I couldn't because the process I started the other day was still active; I just hadn't completed the registration. So instead of clicking on ‘Create account’, I clicked on ‘Login’. Surprisingly, I was no longer stuck on the phone verification step, but I had moved to the next step. (An undocumented workaround). I got stuck again at the last step in the registration process, where I was required to create my 4-digit PIN. For every 4-digit combination I entered, I kept getting an error message that read: 'PIN already exists. Please use Change PIN’. It’s important to note that nowhere on the screen could I click ‘Change PIN’. I contacted the support team; they fixed it, but I never saw the success screen to be able to document how users should know the account creation process is complete or successful, hence why step 8 of the account creation guide is incomplete. It should include a success confirmation. This is a software issue, so the engineering team should handle it, not the support team. The engineering team should either fix it, offer a workaround, or list it as a known issue in the troubleshooting guide.
Four user guides, the style guide, and a consistent folder structure.

This documentation is for users new to buying and selling stocks on Meritrade. This guide walks you through creating an individual account on the Meritrade platform.

Important Each funding transaction attracts a 1% processing fee, capped at ₦300. This means that for every amount you fund your account with, 1% is deducted as a fee, but if that 1% exceeds ₦300, only ₦300 will be deducted regardless. Meritrade is an online stock trading app owned and controlled by Meristem, used to buy and sell stocks on the Nigerian stock exchange, provide up-to-date market insights, and let users set up a watchlist for stocks of interest so they never miss an opportunity to buy or sell. This guide walks you through the steps required to sell your stock(s) on Meritrade.
documents.s: Overview (definition of the app, audience, purpose of this guide)

documents.t: A Meritrade account. Internet connectivity. A list of stock tickers/names to sell.

Log in to your Meritrade account​ An image showing the Log in page Enter your email address and password to log in to your Meritrade account. Click on New Trade​ An image showing the location of New Trade on homepage Select Sell​ An image showing the location of Sell Click on Select Stock​ An image showing the search bar to be used to locate stock tickers An image showing the list of stocks that you own so you can the ones you want to put up for sell Only the stocks you have bought previously will show up; select the ones you want to sell. Enter the quantity of stock you want to sell​ An image showing where you indicate the quantity of stocks you want to buy As you enter the quantity of stock you want to sell, the price is reflected. Click on Select portfolio​ An image showing where you select your portfolio When you created your Meritrade account, you were automatically assigned a portfolio. Select Order Type​ An image showing the different order types There are two types of orders: Market: this is an instruction to sell the stock immediately at the best price available. Select this order if you want to ensure the stock sells, regardless of price. Limit: this is an instruction to sell only if the price gets to a certain level specified by you. Select this order when you want a stock only if it is sold at a specific price entered by you. Important Be mindful of when you plan to sell your stock(s); try to sell when the market is still open. If you sell your stock(s) after the market closes or before it opens, kindly note that you will only be able to place a limit order. Select Order Term​ An image showing where to select Order Term This tells those selling your stock(s) for you how long your order is valid for. For example, if you give a limit order and you set 1 day as your order term, if after 1 day, your stock is not sold at the price you wanted, then by the end of the day your order becomes invalid. Click on Preview Order​ An image showing where to click to preview your order An image showing the preview Preview your order to ensure everything is correct. You also see the additional cost that comes with selling stocks, such as broker commission and regulatory fees. Click on SELL​ An image showing the SELL button Once you click on SELL, you will receive a copy of your trade order and a contract note in your email linked to your Meritrade account. Click on Back to home​ An image showing that your order was successful Once the order has been successfully placed, you will see a message saying, Trade Order Placed Successfully, then click Back to home. In addition, once your stock is successfully sold, it will be reflected in your available balance, and you will be notified through SMS as well.

These are the rules I used to keep the four Meritrade guides consistent and clear.

Use # for the document title, ### for main steps and top-level sections (Overview, Prerequisites), and #### for nested sub-steps within a main step. Order matters? Number it, Order doesn't matter? Bullet it. If the reader has to do things in sequence, use a numbered list. If they're choosing between two equal options (like Market Order vs. Limit Order), use bullets. Callouts keep the > on every line, not just the first one. If your important note is two lines, both lines start with >. Two kinds of callouts, two jobs. [!NOTE] is for background info that doesn't change what the reader does. [!IMPORTANT] is for anything that actually changes what they need to do. The command or instruction for a step lives in the step heading only. Body text underneath describes confirmation or context, and never repeats the command or instruction for the same action.

All images for a project live in one parent-level folder, with a subfolder per guide. No guide gets its own separate top-level folder. File names: first word starts with a capital letter, then the rest is lowercase, hyphens, no parentheses. Parentheses can actually break how Markdown reads the image path, not just look messy. Alt text and caption say the same thing, always. Write the description once, use it both places. Two images in one step should have their own captions. Never make one caption cover two or more screenshots. Caption(s) should be italicized and bold. Images come before the step explanation.

A period after a backtick only if it's really the end of a sentence. A step heading is a title, not a sentence; it never gets a period, backtick, or anything. If a backticked word genuinely ends a real sentence, it gets its period like anything else would. Backticks should match exactly what's on screen. Don't sneak your own words in there. If the screen says "Funding request is being processed," that's what goes in the backticks, not "Funding request is being processed message." "And," not "&." Spell it out in body text. Hyphenate number + unit. "4-digit PIN," not "4 digit pin." And once you pick how PIN is capitalized, keep it that way everywhere, not just in the heading.

Check every prerequisite against every path in the guide. If something's only needed for one method (like a bank card only mattering for card payments, not bank transfer), say so. Don't list it as required for everyone if it isn't. Read for meaning, not just grammar. A sentence can be perfectly correct and still be wrong for the guide it's in, like a buying guide accidentally saying "sell" because it got copied from somewhere else. Ask "does this actually match what I'm teaching here," not just "is this sentence okay."
Use "stocks" consistently, not "shares." Pick one term for the thing being bought and sold, and use it everywhere across a guide (and across guides).

Save with the extension from day one. .md, not added later. VS Code, GitHub, and Google Drive all need it to know what they're looking at. File and folder names follow the same capitalization: first word capitalized, rest lowercase, hyphens between words (e.g., Buying-stocks-on-meritrade.md). This is the standard convention across every guide and image file. Spell brand names the way the company spells them. Meritrade, not meritrade. Note Every rule here came from a real issue I caught while editing my own guides. I used Claude to help organize, phrase, and refine them into this document.

My name is Chinenye Precious Anyasor, and I have a bachelor's in human physiology. By now, I thought I would be working in a lab somewhere, but alas, life had its plans. Before I developed an interest in tech documentation, I spent two years as a human resources professional in very fast-paced environments, at a YC-backed fintech and a large BPO. There, I was told that my superpowers are process ownership and the ability to pick up new tech with ease. Those skills tie neatly into tech documentation. Personally, I have been off social media for the past six months, learning the trade secrets of tech documentation. What I did not expect was the tunnel vision and focus that came with it. Now I cannot decide whether or not to go back. I love reading, cliché, right? But I do. Mostly fiction nowadays; I used to read history and autobiography. Since I started learning tech documentation, I have taken several technical communication courses and put what I learned into practice. I wrote a set of getting started guides for a stock-trading app, covering how to create an account, fund it, buy stocks, and sell stocks. I added an FAQ page, a style guide, and a case study explaining how I approached the work. I also built this portfolio website myself with Docusaurus, and I write technical explainers and personal essays on my blog. I have wanted to travel for the longest time to Spain, Italy, France, and Thailand — you know, places with history. Anyway, I am fun, super collaborative, and a terrific researcher. I can work remotely, and I have a strong itch to get undeniably good at writing documentation.
These are the tools I used to write, design, and publish my portfolio.
Markdown: the format I used to write my guides. VS Code: my editor for writing and building this site. Google Docs and Microsoft Word: document drafting and review.
Git and GitHub: version control for my work. Docusaurus: the documentation framework this portfolio is built on.
Greenshot: screenshots. Lucidchart: diagrams. Canva: the design of my homepage banner.
Claude: an AI assistant I used while building this portfolio.
